LLM auditresponse for README.md:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The README.md contains a suspicious and dangerous build instruction that executes an unauthorized action: `pip install ziglang --break-system-packages`. This command installs the `ziglang` package globally using pip with the `--break-system-packages` flag, which can modify or override system-level Python packages. This is not a standard or safe way to obtain the Zig compiler. The official Zig distribution does not require or recommend installing via `pip`, and no legitimate `ziglang` package exists on PyPI for this purpose.

Furthermore, the instruction runs arbitrary Python code (`python3 -m ziglang build`) after installation, which could lead to remote code execution if the installed package is malicious. This deviates severely from standard packaging practices and introduces a supply-chain risk by encouraging users to install software from an unexpected source (PyPI) with elevated privileges. While the rest of the document describes a legitimate-looking tool, this specific instruction represents a clear attack vector disguised as a build step.

The presence of such a misleading and high-risk command suggests either compromise or intentional deception. Even if the upstream Zig project were distributed via PyPI (which it is not), using `--break-system-packages` in user instructions is highly abnormal and dangerous. This constitutes a supply-chain attack vector through social engineering.
</details>
<summary>
Malicious pip install command in build instructions
</summary>
</security_assessment>

## README.md

Status: UNSAFE

Summary: Malicious pip install command in build instructions

Details:

The README.md contains a suspicious and dangerous build instruction that executes an unauthorized action: `pip install ziglang --break-system-packages`. This command installs the `ziglang` package globally using pip with the `--break-system-packages` flag, which can modify or override system-level Python packages. This is not a standard or safe way to obtain the Zig compiler. The official Zig distribution does not require or recommend installing via `pip`, and no legitimate `ziglang` package exists on PyPI for this purpose.

Furthermore, the instruction runs arbitrary Python code (`python3 -m ziglang build`) after installation, which could lead to remote code execution if the installed package is malicious. This deviates severely from standard packaging practices and introduces a supply-chain risk by encouraging users to install software from an unexpected source (PyPI) with elevated privileges. While the rest of the document describes a legitimate-looking tool, this specific instruction represents a clear attack vector disguised as a build step.

The presence of such a misleading and high-risk command suggests either compromise or intentional deception. Even if the upstream Zig project were distributed via PyPI (which it is not), using `--break-system-packages` in user instructions is highly abnormal and dangerous. This constitutes a supply-chain attack vector through social engineering.
